{{Short description|English mathematician}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=October 2019}}
'''William Neile''' (7 December 1637 – 24 August 1670) was an [[United Kingdom|English]] [[mathematician]] and founder member of the [[Royal Society]]. His major mathematical work, the [[Arc length|rectification]] of the [[semicubical parabola]], was carried out when he was aged nineteen, and was published by [[John Wallis]]. By carrying out the determination of [[arc length]]s on a curve given algebraically, in other words by extending to [[algebraic curve]]s generally with [[Cartesian geometry]] a basic concept from [[differential geometry]], it represented a major advance in what would become [[infinitesimal calculus]]. His name also appears as Neil.

==Life==
Neile was born at [[Bishopsthorpe]], the eldest son of [[Paul Neile|Sir Paul Neile]] MP for Ripon and Newark. His grandfather was [[Richard Neile]], the [[Archbishop of York]].<ref name = DNB/> He entered [[Wadham College, Oxford]] as a [[gentleman-commoner]] in 1652, matriculating in 1655. He was taught by [[John Wilkins]] and [[Seth Ward (bishop)|Seth Ward]].<ref name = DNB>{{DNB Cite|wstitle=Neile, William|volume=40}}</ref>

In 1657, he became a student at the [[Middle Temple]]. In the same year he gave his exact rectification of the semicubical parabola and communicated his discovery to [[William Brouncker, 2nd Viscount Brouncker|William Brouncker]], [[Christopher Wren]] and others connected with [[Gresham College]].  His demonstration was published by Wallis in ''De Cycloide'' (1659). The general formula for rectification by [[definite integral]] was in effect discovered by [[Hendrik van Heuraet]] in 1659. In 1673 Wallis asserted that [[Christiaan Huyghens]], who was advancing his own claim to have influenced Heuraet, was also slighting the priority of Neile.<ref name = DNB/><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www-groups.dcs.st-and.ac.uk/~history/Biographies/Heuraet.html|title = Hendrik van Heuraet - Biography}}</ref>

Neile was elected a fellow of the Royal Society on 7 January 1663 and a member of the council on 11 April 1666. He entered the debate on the theory of [[Motion (physics)|motion]], as a critic of the [[empiricist]] stance of other members. His own theory of motion was held up from publication by unfavourable peer review by Wallis, in 1667; a revision was communicated to the society on 29 April 1669. Neile objected to Wren's 1668 work on [[collision]] as lacking discussion of causality: he asked for discussion of the nature of [[momentum]]. His own work was much influenced by ideas drawn from the ''[[De Corpore]]'' of [[Thomas Hobbes]].<ref name = DNB/><ref>[[Andrew Pyle (philosopher)|Andrew Pyle]] (editor), ''Dictionary of Seventeenth Century British Philosophers'' (2000), article on Neile, pp. 602-3.</ref><ref>Jon Parkin, ''Science, Religion and Politics in Restoration England: Richard Cumberland's De Legibus Naturae'' (1999), pp. 136-7.</ref>

He made astronomical observations with instruments erected on the roof of his father's residence, the “Hill House” (later called Waltham Place) at [[White Waltham]] in [[Berkshire]], where he died at the age of 32. A white marble monument in the parish church of White Waltham commemorates him and an inscribed slab in the floor marks his burial-place. He belonged to the [[Privy Council of the United Kingdom|privy council]] of [[Charles II of England|King Charles II]].<ref name = DNB/>
